verdicts.why: Whether `tableIn.available()` can return 0 with bytes still pending depends entirely on TruncatedInputStream.available() and on the stream type the caller wraps (ValueReader is constructed with a caller-supplied DataInputStream at line 57); neither TruncatedInputStream nor any caller is present under the target path, so the loop's correctness cannot be decided from these files.

A `-SNAPSHOT` version on the development trunk is normal Maven practice and the pom itself configures maven-release-plugin (pom.xml:737), which strips `-SNAPSHOT` when a release is cut, so this is not a release manifest; the stated mechanism is also factually wrong, since a project's own version string does not change which source the build compiles.

groovy-all is declared only as a dependency of the groovy-maven-plugin (pom.xml:595-604) to execute the project's own script `generate_amqp_sources.groovy` (pom.xml:633) over the project's own codegen spec; it never enters the published artifact and processes no attacker-controlled input, so there is no attacker and no impact — only a version-currency preference.

readBytes() allocates `new byte[(int)contentLength]` at line 88 from a peer-supplied 32-bit length before `in.readFully(buffer)` at line 89 verifies any data exists, and the only guard (`contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE`, line 87) still permits ~2 GB, so ~9 bytes of wire data can force a multi-gigabyte allocation.

The jetty-servlet dependency carries `<scope>test</scope>` (pom.xml:454-457), so it is never shipped nor reachable by any attacker of the library, and the claim itself concedes there is no production impact; the version string `9.4.58.v20250814` also shows that line was still receiving builds, contradicting the end-of-life premise.

The evidence's central assertion — "No bounds checking is performed on contentLength before allocation" — is contradicted by the explicit guard `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` at line 87, and the specific value the claim names (Integer.MAX_VALUE) takes the else branch at line 91 and throws UnsupportedOperationException instead of allocating anything.

The 64-bit seconds value at line 269 is fully peer-controlled with or without overflow, so wrapping grants the attacker no capability: any negative or arbitrary Date the overflow could produce is reachable directly by sending that value (e.g. a negative long), and no legitimate timestamp is anywhere near the ~9.2e15 threshold.

Same as the other timestamp claims: `in.readLong()` at line 269 is already attacker-chosen, so the multiplication wrap adds no exploit capability — an attacker wanting a specific bogus Date simply sends that value directly rather than a value that wraps to it.

The claimed impact on expiration/scheduling/time-based authorization does not follow: readTimestamp() at line 269 returns whatever the peer encodes regardless of overflow, so removing the wrap would not restrict the attacker's choice of Date at all — there is no privilege boundary crossed by the multiplication.

The quoted code is exact: line 86 reads an unsigned 32-bit length from the wire and line 88 allocates a byte array of that size before line 89 reads any payload, and the line 87 guard admits values up to 2,147,483,646, so a short crafted frame can trigger a ~2 GB allocation attempt.

Identical to the other timestamp claims — line 269 multiplies a value the peer already fully controls, so the wrap corrupts nothing the peer could not corrupt by sending the wrapped value outright; the claim also miscomputes the threshold as 9,223,372,036,854 (Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 is ~9,223,372,036,854,775).

The title's "Silent Type Corruption" is false: line 217 throws MalformedFrameException, so an unrecognised type byte fails closed and no value is corrupted; the residual point — that the byte value is absent from the message — is a diagnostics/readability preference with no attacker capability.

The cycle is real and unguarded: readFieldValue (line 158) case 'F' calls readTable (line 181) which calls readFieldValue (line 150), and case 'A' calls readArray (line 184) which calls readFieldValue (line 245), with no depth counter anywhere in the file; each nesting level costs only ~5-6 wire bytes, so a modest payload drives thousands of frames.

Case 'D' reads into a fixed `new byte[4]` at line 173 and the scale is a single unsigned byte at line 172, so the BigInteger is always 4 bytes — the claim itself concedes this and relocates the attack to a hypothetical future "extension of the protocol", meaning there is no attacker path in the code as written.

Every line reference checks out — readFieldValue (158-221) reaches readTable at 181 and readArray at 184, and both re-enter readFieldValue at 150 and 245 respectively — and neither readTable (139-155) nor readArray (237-249) carries any depth limit, so nesting depth is bounded only by payload size.

The description of line 87 is accurate — `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE` permits up to Integer.MAX_VALUE-1 — and the allocation at line 88 precedes the readFully at line 89, so the declared length is never validated against how much data actually follows.

readTable at 139 calls readFieldValue at 150, which dispatches back into readTable at 181 and readArray at 184, and readArray at 237 calls readFieldValue at 245; no method in the file tracks or caps depth, and the tableLength==0 early return at line 143 only stops empty tables, not nested ones.

The quoted call sites are exact (readTable's readFieldValue call at line 150, cases 'F'/'A' at lines 181/184) and no depth guard exists; a nested-table level costs about six wire bytes, so ten thousand levels fit well inside a normal frame (the only slip is naming it StackOverflowException rather than StackOverflowError).

A GPG key ID is public by construction — it is embedded in every published .asc signature and on public keyservers — so `<gpg.keyname>6026DFCA</gpg.keyname>` discloses nothing; forging signatures requires the private key, and anyone holding it can derive the key ID trivially, so the stated impact does not follow.

`new String(b, "utf-8")` at line 70 uses Java's REPLACE decoding, which is deterministic and never throws, and the peer already controls the entire short-string, so malformed UTF-8 yields no string it could not produce directly as well-formed UTF-8 — no additional attacker capability, and no second decoder in this file to disagree with.

Confirmed by the code: the mutual recursion readFieldValue(158) -> readTable(181)/readArray(184) -> readFieldValue(150/245) has no depth bound, and readTable/readArray impose only a byte-length truncation, not a nesting limit, so a broker or MITM feeding nested 'F'/'A' values drives the stack to exhaustion.

Line 88 allocates the full declared length before any payload is read at line 89, and the line 87 check only excludes values >= Integer.MAX_VALUE, so a ~2 GB declaration in a tiny frame reaches the allocator (the claim's only imprecision is saying "up to Integer.MAX_VALUE" instead of MAX_VALUE-1).

Factually wrong on two counts: `String(byte[], String charsetName)` is not a deprecated constructor (the deprecated byte[] constructors are the hibyte ones), and it never falls back to the platform default — it throws the checked UnsupportedEncodingException, which cannot occur here because "utf-8" is a required charset on every JVM.

Line 269's input is an arbitrary peer-supplied 64-bit seconds count; values large enough to overflow (>~9.2e15 seconds, hundreds of millions of years) are already meaningless, and the wrapped Date is no more wrong or more reachable than the unwrapped one, so the claim names a wrap with no stated impact and no capability gain.

Same build-time-only surface as K03 — groovy-all is a groovy-maven-plugin dependency (pom.xml:595-604) running the project's own script, absent from the shipped jar and fed only project-controlled input — and the evidence is self-contradictory, asserting that 2.4.21 reached end-of-life in 2015, which precedes the existence of that patch release.

slf4j-api (pom.xml:376-379) is a logging facade with no vulnerability named by the claim, no attacker and no exposed input path; "a newer major version exists" is a dependency-currency preference, not a defect, and 1.7.x is retained precisely because 2.x changes the binding mechanism and would break consumers.
